content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 1997 for the surveillance of drug resistance in tuberculosis, providing a framework for monitoring and addressing this critical public health issue. 2. In 2003, WHO updated its guidelines for tuberculosis drug resistance surveillance, reflecting advancements in methodologies and global health priorities. 3. The fourth edition of the WHO guidelines for tuberculosis drug resistance surveillance was released in 2009, incorporating the latest evidence and practices to enhance global monitoring efforts. 4. In 2008, WHO issued a policy statement on the use of molecular line probe assays for the rapid screening of patients at risk of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB), emphasizing the importance of early detection. 5. The Xpert MTB/RIF assay, an automated real-time nucleic acid amplification technology, was endorsed by WHO in 2013 for the rapid and simultaneous detection of tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance in both pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB cases in adults and children. 6. WHO released an implementation manual for the Xpert MTB/RIF assay in 2014, providing technical and operational guidance for its practical application in clinical and laboratory settings. 7. The WHO/IUATLD Global Project on Anti-Tuberculosis Drug Resistance Surveillance published its first report in 1997, highlighting the global burden of drug-resistant TB. 8. The second report from the WHO/IUATLD Global Project, released in 2000, detailed the prevalence and trends of anti-tuberculosis drug resistance worldwide. 9. The third global report on anti-tuberculosis drug resistance surveillance was published by WHO in 2004, offering updated data and insights into the evolving epidemiology of drug-resistant TB. 10. In 2008, WHO released the fourth global report on anti-tuberculosis drug resistance surveillance, further advancing the understanding of this critical public health challenge. 11. The 2010 Global Report on Multidrugand Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (M-/XDR-TB) provided a comprehensive overview of surveillance and response efforts worldwide. 12. WHO's Global Tuberculosis Report 2014 presented the latest data on TB incidence, prevalence, and mortality, as well as progress in combating the disease. 13. In 2014, WHO published standards and benchmarks for tuberculosis surveillance and vital registration systems, including a checklist and user guide to improve data quality and reliability. 14. The 2013 revision of the WHO framework for tuberculosis definitions and reporting provided updated guidance for consistent and accurate data collection and analysis. 15. WHO and UNAIDS released updated guidelines for second-generation HIV surveillance in 2013, emphasizing the importance of understanding the epidemic's dynamics. 16. In 2012, WHO issued guidelines on collaborative TB/HIV activities, targeting national programs and stakeholders to enhance integrated care and prevention efforts. 17. A 2009 study by Lönnroth et al. emphasized the inclusion of risk factors, socioeconomic status, and health-seeking behavior in tuberculosis prevalence surveys to improve understanding of disease determinants. 18. WHO's 2011 handbook on tuberculosis prevalence surveys provided detailed instructions for conducting these studies, ensuring methodological rigor and reliability. 19. The Global Laboratory Initiative published the Mycobacteriology Laboratory Manual in 2014, offering comprehensive guidance on laboratory procedures for TB diagnosis and research. 20. A training package on the Xpert MTB/RIF assay was developed by the Global Laboratory Initiative in 2014 to support capacity building and effective implementation. 21. WHO updated interim critical concentrations for first-line and second-line drug susceptibility testing (DST) in 2012, reflecting advancements in diagnostic accuracy. 22. Ethical considerations in second-generation surveillance were addressed by WHO in 2004, highlighting the importance of balancing public health needs with individual rights. 23. The first edition of New Ethics for the Public’s Health, published by Oxford University Press in 1999, explored ethical frameworks for addressing public health challenges. 24. WHO's 2007 publication on ethical considerations in pandemic influenza response provided guidance for developing equitable and effective public health strategies. 25. The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences released international ethical guidelines for epidemiological studies in 2009, promoting ethical research practices. 26. WHO's 2010 guidance on the ethics of tuberculosis prevention, care, and control emphasized the need for ethical decision-making in TB programs. 27. A 2012 article by Coleman et al. discussed the role of informed consent in tuberculosis testing and screening, underscoring its importance in patient-centered care. 28. WHO's 2012 Tuberculosis Laboratory Biosafety Manual outlined best practices for ensuring safety in TB diagnostic and research laboratories. 29. The 2004 edition of Toman’s Tuberculosis: Case Detection, Treatment, and Monitoring provided a question-and-answer format to address key clinical and operational issues in TB management. 30. WHO's 1991 manual on sample size determination in health studies, authored by Lwanga and Lemeshow, remains a foundational resource for designing robust research studies. 31. A 2015 study by Zignol et al. presented evidence from global surveillance on multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in children, highlighting the unique challenges in this population. 32. WHO's guidelines for the safe shipment of infectious materials emphasized compliance with international regulations to prevent risks associated with transporting M. tuberculosis cultures.
